## Overview

In Parts 1–4 the sensitivity (Se) and specificity (Sp) of a test were treated as
known numbers. Here we admit that we are *uncertain* about them, and express that
uncertainty with explicit Beta distributions: our **credal state**.

$$
\text{Se} \sim \text{Beta}(a_{se}, b_{se}), \qquad
\text{Sp} \sim \text{Beta}(a_{sp}, b_{sp}) \quad\text{(independent)},
$$

and we study the induced posterior distribution of the predictive values in a target
population whose prevalence $\pi$ is specified:

$$
\text{PPV}(\text{Se}, \text{Sp}; \pi) = \frac{\pi\,\text{Se}}{\pi\,\text{Se} + (1-\pi)(1-\text{Sp})}.
$$

If we also observe a 2×2 table of the test against the true outcome (TP, FN among
diseased; TN, FP among non-diseased), the Beta priors update conjugately:
$\text{Se} \mid \text{data} \sim \text{Beta}(a_{se}+\text{TP},\, b_{se}+\text{FN})$, and
$\text{Sp} \mid \text{data} \sim \text{Beta}(a_{sp}+\text{TN},\, b_{sp}+\text{FP})$.

| Part | Idea |
|------|------|
| 5 | **Your team builds the components** of the `screenbayes` package and its Shiny app (class hackathon, see `HACKATHON.md`): Beta utilities, predictive values, point estimates (mean, median, MAP), interval estimates (equal-tailed, HDI, HPD region) and a plot |
| 6 | **You use the app** to depict and explore posterior distributions, compare estimators, and choose target populations |

### How this problem set is organised

The code lives in the R package **screenbayes** (the repository this document sits in).
There are six teams, and each team owns one file in `R/`:

| Team | File | Functions |
|------|------|-----------|
| 1 | `R/team1_beta.R` | `beta_from_mean_n`, `beta_mean`, `beta_median`, `beta_mode`, `update_beta` |
| 2 | `R/team2_predictive.R` | `ppv_fn`, `npv_fn`, `ppv_predictive` |
| 3 | `R/team3_intervals.R` | `eti_beta`, `hdi_beta`, `eti_draws`, `hdi_draws` |
| 4 | `R/team4_map_hpd.R` | `map_kde`, `hpd_region`, `prob_exceeds` |
| 5 | `R/team5_populations.R` | `stratum_prevalence`, `stratum_beta`, `prev_draws` |
| 6 | `R/team6_plot.R` | `posterior_plot` (four layers) |

Section 5.*N* below belongs to team *N*: your team implements those functions
(the tests in `tests/testthat/` tell you when you are done) and **each member
writes up the section's questions individually**. Section 5.7 and all of Part 6 are
individual work, using the integrated app after the hackathon.

Until a function is implemented, the matching panel of the app shows a
"Not yet working" message, so the app comes to life as teams merge.

```{r setup}
library(screenbayes)
library(dplyr); library(ggplot2); library(tidyr)
bw <- bw_data()
set.seed(260)
r3 <- function(x) round(x, 3)
```

### 5.2 Predictive values

**Team 2.** Implement `ppv_fn()`, `npv_fn()` (vectorised) and `ppv_predictive()` in `R/team2_predictive.R`. The last returns

$$
P(D \mid T^+, \text{data}) = \frac{\pi\, E[\text{Se}]}{\pi\, E[\text{Se}] + (1-\pi)\, E[1-\text{Sp}]}
$$

for a **new** person who tests positive, where the expectations are taken over the
Beta distributions for Se and Sp.

**Question.** Using the law of total probability, explain in two or three sentences why
$P(T^+ \mid D, \text{data}) = E[\text{Se} \mid \text{data}]$. Why does this make the
predictive PPV a ratio of posterior *means* rather than the posterior mean of
$\text{PPV}(\text{Se}, \text{Sp}; \pi)$?

### 5.4 The mode (MAP) and the HPD region from draws

**Team 4.** Implement `map_kde()`, `hpd_region()` and `prob_exceeds()` in `R/team4_map_hpd.R`. The HPD
(highest posterior density) **region** is the set of values whose density exceeds a
threshold $c$, with $c$ chosen so that the set has posterior mass `mass`. It is the
smallest-*size* set holding that mass, and it can have several pieces.

**Questions.**

should be a little above 0.5. Give one reason (hint: where does the kernel density
estimate misbehave?) and propose one fix in a sentence (don't implement it).

### 5.6 The plot

**Team 6.** Complete the four TODO layers in `posterior_plot()` (`R/team6_plot.R`) so that the
figure shows: the HPD region shaded, one vertical line per point estimate, bars
showing each interval method below the curve, and (optionally) a threshold.

**Question.** Run the code below, which uses the test "previous premature labour" with
flat priors and the observed counts, in the population with prevalence 0.08. Paste the plot
and describe in two sentences how the three point estimates and the three intervals
compare to each other.

```{r p5-6}
k <- test_counts("ptl_pos")
se_post <- update_beta(1, 1, k[["tp"]], k[["fn"]])
sp_post <- update_beta(1, 1, k[["tn"]], k[["fp"]])
d <- post_draws(20000, se_post, sp_post, prev = 0.08)
s <- summarise_posterior(d$ppv, mass = 0.95)
posterior_plot(d$ppv, s, xlab = "PPV at prevalence 0.08", threshold = 0.25)
```
